doc.title: Peter Appleyard interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 4, 2012

title: Cousin Brian says he talks 'posh': accent and class in Britain
summary: Rowe notes Appleyard's accent is not very English; he tells of his cousin's remark and explains the word 'posh' and class distinction.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Yeah. You know you don’t have a very distinctive English accent.

You know it’s funny that you say this because where I come from their dialect or whatever you could call it, accent, is very broad. Like for instance if I’d grown up around there I’m sure I would have adopted it. I go back and I can hear my accent slipping into that way of speaking. And it’s funny you know, about four years ago I went back and I invited my four cousins to come to see me play. They’d never seen me play. And so one of them, Brian, said, to me, “Peter, what happened to your accent? You don’t talk like us anymore. You’re talking posh now.” I said, “Brian, I’ve been gone for 50, 60 years, living with Canadian people, married to a Canadian girl, and consequently I haven’t deliberately tried to lose my accent.” “Ah, well, I can’t understand what you’re saying anymore.”
He said you were talking what?

Posh. Well you know in Britain it’s like in the line of “My Fair Lady” they were singing and the Professor, Higgins, says you can always identify an Englishman the minute he opens his mouth, you can immediately identify him. It’s like, and it still is to a certain extent, a class distinction there. You know if you go to a proper school, I would say old chap. It would be actual boy and jolly good show, you know this kind of an accent, a southern or sophisticated accent, which comes probably with the schools and the exposure that these people get. And maybe that type of an Englishman, like ultra-rich or
whatever, has this accent. And it immediately identifies him, that he went to a good college, and so consequently in comes this little bit of prejudice you know.
So parch? I’m not sure what the word was that you used. You’re speaking —
It’s like some rich, posh person.
And anyway I’ve survived it. I go back, and they can still understand me.
